FILE NO.:

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE

BETWEEN:

Plaintiff

– and –

Etienne Fortin aka Brother
Etienne,           St. Joseph’s Training School, Les Frères des écoles
chrétiennes d’Ottawa Ltée, The Roman Catholic Episcopal Corporation of Ottawa
and Her Majesty The Queen in Right of Ontario

)

HEARD:
January 17, 2011

DECISION ON MOTION

Hennessy J.

[
1
]

The action arises from claims of historical
sexual abuse.  The plaintiff alleges that the defendant sexually assaulted him
over a number of years while he was a resident in a detention facility. Without
the plaintiff knowing, the defendant died prior to the commencement of the
action.  Accordingly, the plaintiff now requests the court to appoint a
litigation administrator for the estate of the deceased defendant.

[
2
]

The defendant, les Frères des écoles chrétiennes
d’Ottawa Ltée (“les Frères”), opposes the appointment since the administration
of the estate was completed almost nine years ago, and in any event, there is
no estate.  They also submit that the appointment is statute-barred under the
Trustee
Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. T.23, and further, that the proposed litigation
administrator is an inappropriate person to be appointed.

The Issues

[
3
]

Pursuant to
rule 9.02
of the
Ontario
Rules of
Civil Procedure
, R.R.O. 1990, Reg. 194, the appointment of a litigation
administrator is discretionary.

[
4
]

In order to determine whether the appointment
should be made in this case, the following issues must be considered:

1.

Is the appointment reasonable?

2.

Does the two-year limitation period for actions
against estates found in
s. 38(3)
of the
Trustee Act
bar the action
against Etienne Fortin?

3.

Is the proposed litigation administrator
appropriate?

[
5
]

Because this motion deals only with the
appointment of the litigation administrator, it is not necessary to make a
finding on the limitation issue.  Similar to a motion for summary judgment, the
limitations issue is analysed only for the purpose of the appointment, not for a
final determination.

Request for the Appointment of a
Litigation Administrator

[
6
]

G.B. resided at St. Joseph’s Training School
(“the school”) in Alfred, Ontario from 1969 to 1970, while he was 15 to 16
years of age.  The school was operated by les Frères and was situated within
the Roman Catholic Episcopal Corporation of Ottawa (“the diocese”).  Etienne
Fortin, also known as Brother Etienne, was a member of les Frères and an
employee of the school.  In April 2009, G.B. commenced an action against
Etienne Fortin, les Frères, the school, the diocese and the Crown, alleging
that he was sexually abused during his time at the school.  When he commenced
his action, the plaintiff was unaware that Etienne Fortin died on February 22,
2002.  In order to properly constitute an action against Etienne Fortin, it is
necessary to have a litigation administrator appointed for the deceased Etienne
Fortin and an amendment to the style of cause reflecting this appointment.

[
7
]

Rules 9.03(3)
and
(5)
of the
Rules of Civil
Procedure
provide that:

(3)
A
proceeding commenced in the name of or against a person who has died before its
commencement shall not be treated as a nullity, but the court may order that
the proceeding be continued by or against the executor or administrator or a
litigation administrator appointed for the purpose of the proceeding and the
title of the proceeding shall be amended accordingly.

(5)
A
proceeding by or against a deceased person or an estate shall not be treated as
a nullity because it was not properly constituted, but the court may order that
the proceeding be reconstituted by analogy to the provisions of this rule.

[
8
]

Sections 38(2)
and
(3)
of the
Trustee Act

state:

(2)
Except in cases of
libel and slander, if a deceased person committed or is by law liable for a
wrong to another in respect of his or her person or to another person’s
property, the person wronged may maintain an action against the executor or
administrator of the person who committed or is by law liable for the wrong.

(3)
An action under
this section shall not be brought after the expiration of two years from the
death of the deceased.

[
9
]

The plaintiff proposes that Mr. Jerome Gardner,
a local lawyer, is a proper person to act as litigation administrator.

Defendant’s Position

[
10
]

Only the defendant, les Frères, responded to
this motion.  It submits that Etienne Fortin had taken a vow of poverty, led an
extremely modest life and did not own any property.  The administration of his
estate was completed in 2002 by the provincial executor. For these reasons, the
defendant argues that it would be unreasonable to appoint a litigation
administrator in this case.

[
11
]

In addition, the defendant argues that the delay
in seeking the appointment of a litigation administrator has not been
explained, and that it is prejudiced in that it cannot conduct a timely
investigation.

[
12
]

The defendant also submits that the
Trustee
Act
prescribes a definite and absolute two-year limitation period for
actions against executors and administrators for torts allegedly committed by
the deceased: see
s. 38(3)
. It argues that this time limit is preserved by
s.
19(1)
(a) of the
Limitations Act, 2002
, S.O. 2002,

c. 24, Sched.
B, which reads:

19.
(1)
A
limitation period set out in or under another Act that applies to a claim to
which this Act applies is of no effect unless,

(a)

the provision establishing it is listed in the Schedule to this Act.

[
13
]

Section 38(3)
of the
Trustee Act
is
listed in the Schedule to the
Limitations Act, 2002
.

[
14
]

Further, the defendant argues that the
transition provisions set out in the
Limitations Act, 2002
, are
inapplicable in the context of an action against an estate. They argue that the
time limit set out in the
Trustee Act

meets an important policy goal of
providing finality to civil claims against an estate, and it applies without
regard to the transition provisions in
s. 24
of the
Limitations Act, 2002
:
see
Bikur Cholim Jewish Volunteer Services v. Langston
(2009),
2009 ONCA 196 (CanLII)
, 94 O.R.
(3d) 401 (C.A.).

[
15
]

Finally, the defendant submits that no special
circumstances exist to relieve the plaintiff of the
Trustee Act

limitation
period.

Moving Party’s Position

[
16
]

The moving party relies primarily on the
decision in the case of
B.L. (P.T.) v. B. (P.) Estate
(2010),
2010 ONSC 878 (CanLII)
, 100 O.R. (3d)
110 (S.C.), to support its argument that an appointment should be made
notwithstanding
s. 38(3)
of the
Trustee Act
.

[
17
]

In her reasons for the decision on a motion for
summary judgment in
B.L. (P.T)
, MacLeod-Beliveau J. found that it was
not plain and obvious that the claim for damages arising from sexual abuse by a
person now deceased was statute-barred by the operation of
s. 38(3)
of the
Trustee
Act
.  Her reasons include a full analysis of the interplay between s. 38(3)
of the
Trustee Act
, and
sections 6
,
7
,
11
and
16
of the
Limitations
Act, 2002
.  MacLeod-Beliveau J. found that it was open to the court to find
that the two year limitation period under s. 38(3) of the
Trustee Act

could be tolled
[1]
in the circumstances of
that case.  A motion for leave to appeal the decision of MacLeod-Beliveau J was
denied: see
2010 ONSC 3614 (CanLII)
, 103 O.R. (3d) 59 (S.C.).

[
18
]

The plaintiffs here argue that there is no
express language in the
Trustee Act
clearly providing that the two year
limitation period prescribed by
s. 38(3)
for the commencement of proceedings
against the estate of deceased persons overrides
s. 16(1)
(h) of the
Limitations
Act, 2002
.
That section states that there shall be no limitation period for
actions arising from sexual assault where one of the parties had the charge of
the person assaulted or was in a position of authority in relation to the
person assaulted.

[
19
]

The plaintiff further argues that the doctrine
of special circumstances allows an action to continue despite the expiry of a
limitation period, and the equitable doctrine of fraudulent concealment applies
to toll the two year limitation period under
s. 38(3)
of the
Trustee Act
.
The plaintiff also argues that he is permitted by
sections 7
and
10
of the
Limitations
Act, 2002
, to rely on a defence of incapacity, which would postpone the
commencement of the limitation period.

Analysis

[
20
]

In
Swain Estate v. Lake of the Woods District
Hospital
(1992),
1992 CanLII 7601 (ON CA)
, 9 O.R. (3d) 74 (C.A.), Arbour J.A., writing for the court,
held that
s. 38(7)
of the
Trustee Act
(now
s. 38(3)
) supercedes the
extended limitation period benefitting minors under the former
Limitations
Act
, R.S.O. 1980, c. 240.   In effect, by this decision, the court allowed
the limitation period in the
Trustee Act
to trump the limitation period
set out in the former
Limitations Act
.

[
21
]

In a case dealing with the starting point for
the running of the limitation period, the court in
Camarata v. Morgan

(2009),
2009 ONCA 38 (CanLII)
, 94 O.R. (3d) 496 (C.A.), held that
s. 38(3)
of the
Trustee Act

does not have the effect of tolling a limitation period.  While s. 38(3) can
effectively shorten what would otherwise be the applicable limitation period as
in
Swain
, it cannot extend the limitation period that would have been
applicable had the deceased not died and been able to carry on with the action.

[
22
]

These two decisions must be read in light of
transition provisions set out in
s. 24(7)
of the
Limitations Act, 2002
,
and in the context of the doctrines of special circumstances and fraudulent
concealment, which may apply in cases arising from sexual assaults. Section
24(7) reads:

(7)
In the
case of a claim based on an assault or sexual assault that the defendant
committed, knowingly aided or encouraged, or knowingly permitted the
defendant’s agent or employee to commit, the following rules apply, even if the
former limitation period expired before January 1, 2004:

1.

If section 10 would apply were the claim based
on an assault or sexual assault that took place on or after the January 1,
2004, section 10 applies to the claim, with necessary modifications.

2.

If no limitation period under this Act would
apply were the claim based on a sexual assault that took place on or after
January 1, 2004, there is no limitation period.

[
23
]

The defendant relies on the decision in
Bikur
Cholim
, in which Rosenberg J.A. held that
s. 38(3)
of the
Trustee Act

applies
without regard to the transition provisions in
s. 24
of the
Limitations Act,
2002
. However, Rosenberg

J.A. also made reference to the case of
Kramarz
v. KMH Cardiology & Diagnostic Centres
(2007),
2007 CanLII 35707 (ON SC)
, 87 O.R. (3d) 120 (S.C.),
in which Lederer J. considered the application of the transitions provisions to
s. 38(3) of the
Trustee Act
.  Lederer J. noted that an alleged sexual
assault, governed by
s. 16(1)
(h) of the
Limitations Act, 2002
, would
fall within s. 24(7)(2) of the transitions provisions.  This subsection is
different from the other transition provisions and was not considered in the
analysis in either the
Bikur Cholim
or

Kramarz
decisions.  As a
result, those cases can be distinguished from the present case, in which the
applicable transition provision is
s. 24(7)
(2) of the
Limitations Act, 2002.

[
24
]

The transition provisions of the 2002

Act
operate and apply to this case.
Section 24(7)
states that the basic two year
limitation period does not run during any time in which the person with the
claim is incapable.  The plaintiff has claimed that he was permanently
incapacitated, and there is a statutory presumption of incapacity in
s. 10(3)

of the
Limitations Act, 2002
. Unless this presumption is displaced,
s.
24(7)
will apply to delay the operation of the two year limitation period in
the
Limitations Act, 2002
.

[
25
]

The plaintiff also alleges that the defendant
was in a position of trust and authority over him when the sexual assaults
allegedly occurred.  If the assaults had occurred after the effective date of
the
Limitations Act, 2002
, they would be governed by
s. 16(1)
(h), which
provides that there is no limitation period in respect of proceedings arising
from a sex assault, if at the time of the assault, one of the parties to it had
charge of the person assaulted or was in a position of trust or authority over
the victim.

[
26
]

The defendant argues that the decision in
B.L.
(P.T.)

cannot be usefully considered here because, unlike in the present case,
the events in
B.L. (P.T.)

took place after the coming-into-force of the
Limitations
Act, 2002
– that is, after January 1, 2004.  To date, there are no
decisions that specifically consider the application or non-application of
s.
16(1)
(h) of the
Limitations Act, 2002
vis-à-vis
s. 38(3)
of the
Trustee
Act
.  If the plaintiff successfully argues that the sub-section applies,
there is no limitation issue.  Although this matter has not been the subject of
a final interpretation, it has been considered as a possible outcome in the
reasons of MacLeod-Beliveau in
B.L. (P.T.)
.

[
27
]

In addition, the plaintiff may be able to rely
on the doctrine of fraudulent concealment, which, if proven, effectively tolls
the two year limitation period in the

Trustee Act
.  In
Giroux Estate
,
Moldaver J.A. defined fraudulent concealment as follows, at para. 22:
“Fraudulent concealment has been defined to include ‘conduct, which, having
regard to some special relationship between the two parties concerned is an
unconscionable thing for one to do towards the other’.”  He went on to hold
that the common law equitable doctrine of fraudulent concealment can be
distinguished from the discoverability doctrine of statutory interpretation and
can be used to toll the two year limitation period prescribed by
s. 38(3)
of
the
Trustee Act
. Thus, if the plaintiff can prove fraudulent
concealment, the limitation period does not operate against him.

[
28
]

There is a separate argument that the doctrine
of special circumstances may operate to relieve the plaintiff of the
s. 38(3)

limitation period.  In
Bikur
, Rosenberg J.A. held that the doctrine of
special circumstances survives the enactment of the
Limitations Act, 2002

for actions governed by limitation periods outside of the
Limitations Act,
2002
.  As with the doctrine of fraudulent concealment, the plaintiff will
be put to the proof of the doctrine should he wish to take advantage of it.

[
29
]

In summary, I find that, if any of the following
arguments are successful, the two year limitation period found in
s. 38(3)
of
the
Trustee Act
will not bar the action against Etienne Fortin:

•

Common law equitable doctrine of fraudulent
concealment;

•

Doctrine of special circumstances;

•

Application of s. 16(1)(h) of the
Limitations
Act, 2002
;

•

Defence of incapacity;

•

Transition provisions of the
Limitations Act,
2002
.

[
30
]

The defendant argued that the appointment was
unreasonable, given that Etienne Fortin left no estate. However, the plaintiff
is not motivated by the existence of an estate to satisfy an award of damages,
but rather by the possible existence of records. This is not an unreasonable
approach to the litigation.

[
31
]

To the extent that these arguments are all live
issues, it is not clear that this action is out of time and as such, a
litigation administrator should be appointed.

Terms of Appointment

[
32
]

The defendant argued that the proposal to
appoint Mr. Jerome Gardner as litigation administrator was inappropriate.
Among other things, the defendant believes him to be a unilingual Anglophone,
while les Frères operated in French.  Counsel for the parties may wish to
propose terms and the name of a mutually acceptable person to be appointed.  If
they cannot agree on an appropriate litigation administrator by June 30, 2011,
they may seek an appointment before me to make submissions.  These submissions
can be made by teleconference.

[
33
]

Order to go allowing for the appointment of a
litigation administrator.  The terms of appointment are adjourned, to be
brought back on three days’ notice but in any event before June 30, 2011.

[
34
]

If counsel cannot agree on costs, they may make
a written submission to me within 21 days of the final decision in this case.
The submissions are to consist of no more than two pages and are to be filed
with the Trial Coordinator’s office.

The Honourable Justice Patricia C.
Hennessy
